html:
The Golden Age of Piracy was the period, roughly 1650 to 1726, when pirates preyed on shipping in the Caribbean, the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean. Its peak ran from about 1716 to 1726.

The War of the Spanish Succession ended in 1713 and left thousands of trained sailors out of work. Many turned pirate. Their base from about 1715 was Nassau on New Providence island in the Bahamas, where no government had any power. It became known as the Republic of Pirates. Captains such as Benjamin Hornigold, Charles Vane and Edward Teach, called Blackbeard, sailed from it. Pirate crews often elected their captains and shared plunder by written articles, which was fairer than life on navy or merchant ships.

They robbed ships bound for Europe with the wealth of the Americas and with enslaved people from Africa (see Atlantic slave trade). The British struck back. In 1718 Woodes Rogers arrived as governor of the Bahamas with a royal pardon for those who gave up. Many accepted, others were hunted down and hanged. Blackbeard was killed in 1718.

In 1720 the trial of Calico Jack Rackham's crew in Jamaica included two women, Anne Bonny and Mary Read, who escaped the rope by claiming to be pregnant. By 1726 the pirate threat had been broken.
